content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical scholarship, 'to know' (Hebrew yada'; Greek ginōskō) symbolizes intimate, experiential, relational knowledge rather than mere intellectual or factual awareness. Applied to God, 'knowing' God means being in a living covenant relationship with Him — personal communion, love, obedience, and fidelity — and God's 'knowing' a person signifies His personal, covenantal acknowledgment of them. This is routinely contrasted in commentaries and lexicons (e.g., TDNT, BDB, TWOT) with the Greek philosophical ideal of detached cognition.", "primary_basis": ["Genesis 4:1 ('Adam knew Eve his wife' — knowledge as intimate union, the paradigm case cited for the relational sense)", "John 17:3 ('This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God')", "Jeremiah 31:34 ('They shall all know me, from the least to the greatest')", "Hosea 6:6 ('I desire... the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings')", "Jeremiah 9:23-24 ('Let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me')", "John 10:14-15 ('I know my own and my own know me, just as the Father knows me')", "Philippians 3:10 ('that I may know him and the power of his resurrection')", "Amos 3:2 ('You only have I known of all the families of the earth')", "Matthew 7:23 ('I never knew you; depart from me')", "1 Corinthians 8:1-3 ('If anyone loves God, he is known by God')", "Galatians 4:9 ('now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God')"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Sexual union: 'to know' as a euphemism for sexual intercourse, treated as the concrete instance of the intimate-union sense.", "basis": ["Genesis 4:1, 4:17, 4:25", "Genesis 19:5, 19:8", "Judges 19:25", "Matthew 1:25", "Luke 1:34 ('since I know not a man')"], "prominence": "dominant"}, {"meaning": "Divine election / foreknowledge: God's 'knowing' someone as His sovereign choosing, setting apart, or covenantal election of them beforehand — prominent especially in Reformed exegesis of Romans.", "basis": ["Amos 3:2", "Jeremiah 1:5 ('Before I formed you in the womb I knew you')", "Romans 8:29 ('those whom he foreknew he also predestined')", "Romans 11:2", "1 Peter 1:2, 1:20", "Matthew 7:23"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Moral experience and autonomy: in the 'tree of the knowledge of good and evil' (Genesis 2-3), 'knowing' is read as experiential acquaintance with evil, moral discernment, or the grasping of autonomous moral authority apart from God.", "basis": ["Genesis 2:9, 2:17", "Genesis 3:5, 3:22", "Deuteronomy 1:39", "Isaiah 7:15-16"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Practical obedience: knowing God defined as doing justice and righteousness — knowledge equated with ethical covenant conduct rather than inner experience.", "basis": ["Jeremiah 22:15-16 ('He judged the cause of the poor and needy... Is not this to know me?')", "Hosea 4:1-2, 4:6", "1 John 2:3-4 ('By this we know that we know him, if we keep his commandments')", "Titus 1:16"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Salvific esoteric knowledge (gnosis): knowledge itself as the saving principle, a reading associated with ancient Gnosticism and rejected by orthodox interpreters, who take 1 Corinthians 8:1 and 1 Timothy 6:20 as polemics against it.", "basis": ["1 Corinthians 8:1 ('knowledge puffs up')", "1 Timothy 6:20 ('what is falsely called knowledge')", "Colossians 2:8, 2:18 (read as anti-proto-gnostic)"], "prominence": "rare"}, {"meaning": "Plain intellectual/factual cognition with no symbolic weight: some occurrences are taken simply as mental awareness of information, and some interpreters caution against over-reading yada'/ginōskō everywhere.", "basis": ["Lexical treatments (BDB, HALOT, BDAG) noting the ordinary cognitive sense in many contexts, e.g., Genesis 12:11, Exodus 1:8, Luke 1:18"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is broad, recognizable consensus across Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox interpretation, and across critical scholarship, that biblical 'knowing' denotes relational, experiential, covenantal intimacy rather than detached intellection; the sexual, elective, ethical, and moral-experience senses are generally treated as context-specific expressions of that same core idea rather than competing definitions. Standard reference works (TDNT s.v. ginōskō; TWOT/BDB s.v. yada') are the usual scholarly anchors. The main live debates concern (a) whether 'foreknew' in Romans 8:29 means elective love or mere prescience (a Calvinist-Arminian dispute) and (b) the precise nuance of the 'knowledge of good and evil' in Genesis 2-3; neither disturbs the overall consensus on the term's relational core."}
